content.value:
There are two fundamental ways to control a motor:

Open-loop means you set a power and hope for the best. No feedback. No correction. If the battery sags or the floor changes, the robot behaves differently.

Closed-loop means you measure what's happening and adjust. You set a target (like an encoder position) and the controller constantly corrects toward it.

Which one will get you to the same spot every time?

First, switch to the Programming Board configuration. In the simulator window, use the Configuration dropdown (top of the window, next to the Op Mode dropdown) and select Programming Board. The board has a single motor named motor, and it does not drive around the field.

Your starter file is a working open-loop drive.

It schedules two commands:

1. A SequentialCommandGroup: WaitUntilCommand to wait for the opmode to go active, then an InstantCommand that sets 0.3 power, a WaitCommand for 2 seconds, and a final InstantCommand that stops the motor.

2. A RunCommand that displays telemetry continuously — position, runtime, and current mode.

Run the OpMode. Press START. Watch the motor's encoder position tick up in telemetry, then hold steady after 2 seconds.

Run it a few times. How consistent is the final tick count?

Now increase the Motor Inertia slider in the simulator's left panel. Run again.

With more inertia, the motors take longer to spin up. The robot covers less distance in the same 2 seconds. The final position changes each run.

Open-loop control is fragile. Any change to the system (battery, load, friction, inertia) changes the result.

This is why we need closed-loop control.

Now switch to closed-loop PositionControl.

In initialize(), after creating the motor, set up the closed-loop controller:

Call motor.setRunMode(Motor.RunMode.PositionControl).

Call motor.resetEncoder().

Call motor.setTargetPosition(1000).

Then replace the SequentialCommandGroup with a RunCommand that calls motor.set(1) every loop.

In PositionControl mode, set(1) is a multiplier — it means drive at full power toward the target. The controller compares the encoder count to 1000 and adjusts power automatically.

Run it multiple times. The final position is the same every time.

Closed-loop control is more accurate and repeatable because it constantly measures and corrects.

The controller sees "I'm at 800 ticks, target is 1000, need 200 more" and keeps driving.

It sees "I'm at 1000, target reached" and stops.

Motor's PositionControl uses the setPositionCoefficient() value (defaults to 0.05). You can adjust it with setPositionCoefficient().

This feedback loop is the foundation of everything that follows: PID, feedforward, and flywheel control.
